pr_title: Avoid the sdslen() on shared.crlf given we know its size beforehand. Improve ~3-4% of cpu cycles to lrange logic
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/redis/redis/issues/10986

Problem description:
Using the lrange benchmarks of redis benchmark ( I was investigating it due to #10981 ) we can see that we're wasting a large ammount of cpu cycles on sdslen() computing the sizes we already know:

```
                           - 77.55% lrangeCommand                                                                                                                                                          ▒
                              - 77.31% addListRangeReply                                                                                                                                                   ▒
                                 + 35.46% addReplyBulkCBuffer                                                                                                                                              ▒
                                 + 21.34% listTypeNext (inlined)                                                                                                                                           ▒
                                 - 11.32% addReply (inlined)                                                                                                                                               ▒
                                      6.55% sdslen (inlined)                                                                                                                                               ▒
                                      0.41% _addReplyToBufferOrList (inlined)                                                                                                                              ▒
                                 + 6.88% _addReplyToBufferOrList (inlined)                                                                                                                                 ▒
                                 + 0.60% addReplyLongLongWithPrefix                                                                                                                                        ▒
                                   0.50% prepareClientToWrite                                                                                                                                              ▒
                                   0.15% listTypeReleaseIterator (inlined)  
```

Fix: 

The fix is a simple replace of using addReply with addReplyProto for the `shared.crlf` related replies. 

-------

On the LRANGE_600 benchmark we get:

benchmark command:
```
redis-benchmark  -n 1000000 --threads 3 "LRANGE" "mylist" "0" "599"
```

Unstable
```
Summary:
  throughput summary: 22055.58 requests per second
  latency summary (msec):
          avg       min       p50       p95       p99       max
        1.585     0.080     1.607     2.391     3.015     4.575
```
New
```
Summary:
  throughput summary: 22821.67 requests per second
  latency summary (msec):
          avg       min       p50       p95       p99       max
        1.623     0.056     1.639     2.375     2.959     7.935
```
pr_comments:
Why is sdslen so slow? It doesn't compute anything, the size is cached. 

I don't like to "burn" the length in every use case, we might as well just use addReplyPoroto and include the crlf in every call. 

Maybe the reason is takes so long is because it's relative to something else that's also very fast...
This also makes little sense to me. sdslen is supposed to be a very fast operation, if this is one is slow it's possible there are a lot of other slow cases.

@sundb That is very interesting (I don't remember, but I have the memory of a goldfish). I suppose it makes intuitive sense that if the item < 64 bytes (i.e. one cache line) the performance will be very similar, but it seems like it's significantly faster. I'm really curious what the disassembled code looks like between those cases. Many systems have built in operators for strlen, so it's possible that the compiler is noticing that the string isn't being mutated (although I'm not sure how) and precomputing the length.

I think it's obvious that for short string sdslen could be slower than strlen. But still it's very fast, so if it consumes significant percentage, I think it's just because the other position is very small too..

@oranagra if we dont inline sdslen we can trace it and annotate properly. Just to double check I've confirmed that indeed there is a large number of sdslen calls during a 1M commands benchmark for LRANGE. ``` funccount "`pwd`/src/redis-server:(lrangeCommand|sdslen)" --pid $(pgrep redis-server) Tracing 2 functions for "/root/redis/src/redis-server:(lrangeCommand|sdslen)"... Hit Ctrl-C to end. ^C FUNC COUNT lrangeCommand 1000000 sdslen 4002707 Detaching... ``` Confirmed also that on the profile it is taking ~4% of cpu cycles ( not inlining should cost a bit in here also ) Focusing on the hot instructions within sdslen we see that the comparison and jump on the `switch(flags&SDS_TYPE_MASK) {` it's what´s costing the majority of the cycles. the jump then leads us to `SDS_TYPE_5_LEN(flags)`

@sundb In your benchmark, compiler might compute `strlen(x)` once and multiply the result with `10000000`. Please take a look at: https://godbolt.org/z/5v4qKdz69 . Looks like compiler gives up this optimization with `sdslen(x)` in your benchmark.

Fun fact: In your snippet above, `len` is not initialized, so, it is undefined behavior. Clang takes advantage of it and just returns 0 without calculating anything :scream: 

----
In general, I think `sdslen()` is definitely faster than `strlen()`.  It can be slower for a short string (maybe) or if `sdslen()` triggers a cache miss but `strlen()` doesn't or when an optimization kicks in same as above etc. These cases should be rare I guess. 

When you are benchmarking, compiler might do some tricks as in above. Another thing that might be confusing is when you are making calls to stdlib functions with compile time constants: 

```c
/* Compiler will optimize away these function calls. */
int a, b;

a = strlen("test");        // No strlen() call, a = 4
b = strcmp("hello", "hi"); // No strcmp() call, b = -1
memcpy(&a, &b, sizeof(b)); // No memcpy() call, single MOV instruction, a = b;
``` 
---
Going back to the issue, I didn't try but I guess this performance difference is visible because it is going to call `sdslen()` 600 times per command and also values are quite small (not sure but are these just 3 bytes?) according to that benchmark right?. Otherwise, `sdslen()` wouldn't be noticeable I think. So, my understanding is `sdslen()` itself is not slow. It is just anything we delete/avoid will help. Even it is a small thing, it is visible because it will be called 600 times per command. So, if this is correct, probably there are more important parts we can avoid/delete in this path, I don't know.

If we want to optimize CRLF, I think adding it automatically inside `addReplyProto()` would be better as Oran mentioned above. I guess we can append it just after calling `memcpy()` for the value. This way we can also avoid bunch of "if checks", so it should make performance even better for this case. If this requires big changes, maybe we can have `addReplyProtoCrlf()` version of it, just an idea.

> @sundb In your benchmark, compiler might compute `strlen(x)` once and multiply the result with `10000000`. Please take a look at: [godbolt.org/z/5v4qKdz69](https://godbolt.org/z/5v4qKdz69) . Looks like compiler gives up this optimization with `sdslen(x)` in your benchmark.
> 
> Fun fact: In your snippet above, `len` is not initialized, so, it is undefined behavior. Clang takes advantage of it and just returns 0 without calculating anything 😱
    
    @tezc Thanks for your reminder, it is indeed optimized by the compiler.
     The compiler uses `imul` to calculate the final result.

> If we want to optimize CRLF, I think adding it automatically inside `addReplyProto()` would be better as Oran mentioned above. 

@tezc there are cases in which there are multiple addReplyProto calls for one line thus completly breaking code logic. Example of https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/networking.c#L886, https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/networking.c#L832, and more...

WRT 
> but I guess this performance difference is visible because it is going to call sdslen() 600 times per command and also values are quite small

Indeed. We're doing 600x more work than required.  

> So, my understanding is sdslen() itself is not slow. It is just anything we delete/avoid will help. 

You're right about the second sentence. but WRT sdslen() usage within shared.crlf reply it's completly useles given we know beforehand the size. 

WRT 
> I don't like to "burn" the length in every use case

@oranagra I would argue/disaggre given it's the way to properly doing with 0 computation involved. We find lots of example in redis code like addReplyNullArray: https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/networking.c#L977, addReplyBool https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/networking.c#L963, etc...

@tezc / @oranagra  In my understanding if we can:

> It is just anything we delete/avoid will help.

without adding any unreadable optimization/logic I would vouch for this type of improvement. 4% free CPU cycles reduction it's a lot and I would say that this "optimization" is the cheapest possible one.

Just to be clear, I'm not against this change. I just wanted to understand why would `sdslen()` cost matters here. Looks like the answer is it is not specific to `sdslen()`. Anything we can avoid will help with the performance as we loop a lot in that benchmark.
@oranagra / @tezc updated changes from using clrf shared object to simply using `\r\n`.
i'll wait a few days before merging it to see if anyone else has some interesting input..
